title: How Carbon Capture and Storage Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant revisit carbon capture and storage (CCS), noting they covered it in an earlier short episode. They discuss the greenhouse effect and rising CO2 emissions since 1972, the three capture methods (post-combustion, pre-combustion, oxyfuel), the oil industry's use of CO2 for enhanced oil recovery, CO2 pipelines and their safety record, transport as gas, liquid or solid, underground storage in basalt and other formations, and ocean storage concerns including carbon sinks and ocean acidification. They also mention a sodium-hydroxide/baking-soda idea attributed to a company called Skymine. The episode closes with a plug for their spoken-word audio book on economics and a listener email from Hannah of Tennessee, who was struck by a side strike of lightning.

segments.title: Opening banter and rerun note
segments.summary: Hosts joke about jute rugs and Berber, then say they are revisiting carbon capture and storage, which they covered in an earlier short episode that did not do it justice.

segments.title: Greenhouse effect and rising CO2 emissions
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm (without it, about minus 22 F), but excess trapped heat is a problem. Greenhouse gas emissions rose from 1972 to 2004, and carbon dioxide roughly doubled in that period.

segments.title: CCS basics and enhanced oil recovery
segments.summary: CCS is defined as capture, separation and transport for storage. The oil and gas industry has used pumped CO2 for decades to repressurize depleted reservoirs and enhance oil recovery, and existing pipelines are already in place.

segments.title: Three capture methods: post-combustion, pre-combustion, oxyfuel
segments.summary: Post-combustion captures CO2 from flue gas at a power plant, using compounds such as a silica-based material. Pre-combustion captures CO2 before fuel is burned, producing hydrogen and CO2 and using amine to hold the CO2. Post-combustion can be retrofitted to old plants, while pre-combustion generally requires new plants. Oxyfuel burns fuel in oxygen, producing steam and CO2 that are separated by cooling and compression.

segments.title: Large emitters and power plant CO2
segments.summary: Power plants are the main focus of capture. The hosts cite a Southern Company plant in Juliette, Georgia, said to emit more CO2 than all of Brazil's power infrastructure, and compare this to the size of Vatican City.

segments.title: CO2 transport and pipeline safety
segments.summary: CO2 can be transported as gas, liquid or solid, with gas being most efficient and solid being costly. Pipeline records show only twelve CO2 pipeline leaks from 1996 to 2006 with no injuries, compared with over five thousand accidents and 107 fatalities for liquid petroleum pipelines. Listener Debbie Ranka wrote a related piece.

segments.title: Underground storage in basalt and risks
segments.summary: Underground storage is preferred over ocean storage. The planet is estimated to hold up to ten trillion tons of CO2 underground, about a hundred years of human emissions. CO2 seeps into porous rock, and basalt converts to limestone when injected. The hosts voice caution about unknown long-term effects. The oldest CO2 storage site is under the seafloor in Norway, about thirteen years old.

segments.title: Ocean storage, carbon sinks and baking soda idea
segments.summary: Ocean storage involves liquefied CO2 pumped into large bags on the abyssal plain, which can hold only a day or ten days of captured carbon. The hosts strongly oppose it, and note Greenpeace's objections. They also describe the ocean as an existing carbon sink where Southern Ocean acidification harms marine life. Skymine's process reacting CO2 with salt, water and sodium hydroxide to form baking soda is discussed.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on CCS and fossil fuels
segments.summary: The hosts argue that carbon capture may distract from harder choices such as electric cars, solar power and biofuels. They end the discussion with jokes about a future CO2 eruption.

segments.title: Audio book plug
segments.summary: Chuck plugs the Stuff You Should Know spoken-word audio book on economics, available in the iTunes store.

segments.title: Hannah of Tennessee's lightning side strike
segments.summary: Listener Hannah describes being struck by a side strike of lightning about half a block away, which left her blinded, deafened and rooted in place, and singed her dog Pucci. Both were checked and reported fine.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to send true stories by email and sign off.
